title: Can You Eat Your Favorite Candy on Your Favorite Day?
statement:
You own `candiesCount[i]` candies of type `i` (types are numbered from 0) and eat them under three rules:

- Eating starts on day 0.
- No candy of type `i` may be eaten while any candy of type `i - 1` is left, so candies go in type order. One day may cover several types.
- Every day you eat at least one candy, until none are left.

Each query `queries[i] = [favoriteType, favoriteDay, dailyCap]` asks: is there some way to follow the rules, never eating more than `dailyCap` candies on a single day, such that at least one candy of type `favoriteType` is eaten on day `favoriteDay`? Return a boolean array holding the answer to each query, in the same order as `queries`.
notes:
## Intuition

Every candy has a fixed position in the eating order: the candies of type `t` occupy positions `prefix[t]` through `prefix[t + 1] - 1`, where `prefix[t]` counts all candies of smaller types. A query only asks whether day `favoriteDay` can reach that block. Eating as fast as allowed gets you there soonest; eating one candy a day keeps you there longest. Any day between those two extremes is achievable, so each query is two comparisons once the prefix sums exist. A brute force would simulate every possible amount eaten before each day, which is hopeless for days up to 10^9.

## Approach

1. Build `prefix`, where `prefix[t]` is the number of candies of types `0..t-1`.
2. For each query, the earliest day that can include type `favoriteType` is `floor(prefix[favoriteType] / dailyCap)`: by the end of that day you can have eaten more than `prefix[favoriteType]` candies.
3. The latest such day is `prefix[favoriteType + 1] - 1`: eating one candy a day, that is the day the last candy of the type goes.
4. Answer `true` exactly when `earliest <= favoriteDay <= latest`.

## Example 1, step by step

`candiesCount = [7,4,5,3,8]` gives `prefix = [0,7,11,16,19,27]`.

- `[0,2,2]`: `earliest = floor(0/2) = 0`, `latest = 7 - 1 = 6`; day 2 fits, so `true`.
- `[4,2,4]`: `earliest = floor(19/4) = 4`; day 2 is too early, so `false`.
- `[2,13,1000000000]`: `earliest = 0`, `latest = 16 - 1 = 15`; day 13 fits, so `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + q): one pass builds the prefix sums and each query takes O(1).
- Space: O(n) for `prefix` (plus the output).

## Pitfalls

- Prefix sums reach 10^10, beyond a 32-bit int; use `long` in Java and `long long` in C.
- Comparing `(favoriteDay + 1) * dailyCap` with the prefix can reach 10^18; dividing as in the reference avoids that overflow.
- Day `favoriteDay` is 0-indexed, so the earliest day uses floor division, not ceiling.
- The latest day is one less than the prefix including the favourite type.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `prefix` | `prefix[t]` = candies of all types before `t` |
| `count` | candies of the type being added |
| `favoriteType`, `favoriteDay`, `dailyCap` | the current query |
| `earliest` | first day a candy of the type can be eaten |
| `latest` | last day a candy of the type can be eaten |
| `answer` | results, one per query |

narration.2: prefix[0] is 0: no candies come before type 0.
narration.3: Walk through the candy counts in type order.
narration.4: Each new entry is the running total of candies of all earlier types.
narration.8: Unpack the favourite type, the target day and the daily limit.
narration.9: Eating dailyCap candies a day, this is the first day that reaches the favourite type.
narration.10: Eating one candy a day, this is the last day the favourite type still has candy.
narration.11: The query succeeds exactly when the target day lies between those two days.
narration.13: Return the answers in query order.
